To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Trout Lake Area is characterized by a strain pattern in which the main direction of finite strain is parallel to layering ( M ), and that this strain pattern is disturbed by "late" faulting.
the hornblende-bearing layers of Trout Lake area are parallel to the layering of a non-principal strain section and that this section is parallel to M.
the lineations are parallel (in the Trout Lake Area) to the direction of finite longitudinal strain parallel to layer.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following: (1) the relationship between hornblende lineated layers and local finite strain parallel to the layers (2) the use of hornblende as an indicator of M in large-scale structures and (3) the interpretation of the areal pattern of the M direction as an indication of rotational faulting.
the structural geology of the Trout Lake area, and its relationship with the Birch Rapids –Wepusko Bay Fault Zone.
the relationship between hornblende lineational fabric and finite strain parallel to layers, and with the strain pattern of large-scale folds.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Trout Lake area (western half) is an area of "complex" strain.
the lineation pattern of the Trout lake Area is a product of two major tectonic episodes: the Hudsonian orogenic event, and a later rotational faulting.
the Trout Lake Area is a region where a major fault zone has been reactivated, and that this reactivation is related to a major angular discontinuity in the lineation pattern.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Trout Lake Area is a "late" tectonic zone.
the Trout Lake Area is a "complex" of large- and medium-scale structures, and that the lineation pattern is controlled by the medium-scale structures.
the Trout Lake Area contains evidence of a major period of tectonism, which was accompanied by intense folding, boudinage and rotational faulting.
The main takeaway from our work is that

hornblende lineated layers can be employed as strain indicators in the study of large scale folds, and the orientation of hornblendes is related to the direction of maximum finite strain parallel to the layering, regardless of whether this is a direction of shortening or extension.
the Trout Lake Area is a good example of the utility of hornblende as a strain marker.
hornblende lineated gneisses are a valuable tool for the study of regional strain patterns.
